title: Bhakti yoga: the nine forms of devotion; the Alvars and Nayanars; Mirabai, Tulsidas, Surdas; kirtan as method (4 of 7)
hook: a hunter who didn't know the rules offers Shiva everything, including his own eye
tomorrow: Bhakti yoga: the nine forms of devotion; the Alvars and Nayanars; Mirabai, Tulsidas, Surdas; kirtan as method (5 of 7)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Alvars, Tamil poet-saints of Vishnu. Andal's garland, and a singer carried in on a priest's shoulders. Your line: love as the road. Today, their neighbors, the saints of Shiva. Day two hundred seventy.

Picture a temple priest in the hills of the south, arriving in the morning to do the worship properly. Everything in order: the water, the flowers, the mantras. And every morning he finds the shrine a mess. Meat on the floor. Water splashed everywhere. Wilted wildflowers. Someone is getting in overnight and defiling it. He's heartbroken. So one night he hides, to catch whoever's doing it. What he sees changes how millions of people think about devotion.
screen: `A PRIEST AND HIS PERFECT RITUAL.` → `EVERY MORNING, A MESS.` → `ONE NIGHT HE HIDES.`

segments.voice: The Nayanars are the Alvars' neighbors: sixty-three Tamil saints of Shiva, living over roughly the same centuries. Their stories were gathered in the twelfth century by the poet Sekkizhar in a book called the Periya Puranam, the great story. Three of them, Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar, left hymns still sung in Shiva temples every day. And one of them is the hunter the priest saw that night. His name was Thinnan. He'd found the Shiva linga in the forest and fallen completely in love. He knew none of the rules. So he worshiped the way a hunter would. He carried water in his own mouth and poured it over the linga. He brought flowers tucked in his hair. He offered the best meat from his hunt, tasted first to make sure it was good. The priest watched, horrified. Then, the story says, one of the eyes on the linga began to bleed. Thinnan didn't hesitate. He cut out his own eye and pressed it into place. The bleeding stopped. Then the other eye began to bleed. He had one eye left, and he needed to find the spot once he was blind, so he put his foot on the linga to mark it and raised the arrow. And Shiva stopped his hand. From that day he's been called Kannappa, the one who gave his eye. The Nayanars include a woman, Karaikkal Ammaiyar, among the earliest poets of all, and a laborer, Nandanar, kept outside the temple, who longed only to see Shiva dance. Love first. Rules, maybe, later.
screen: `SIXTY-THREE SAINTS OF SHIVA.` · `A HUNTER WHO KNEW NO RULES.` · `THE EYE THAT BLED.` · `KANNAPPA, WHO GAVE HIS EYE.` · then, large: `LOVE AS THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Sit, and think of the way you express love when nobody's grading you. Maybe clumsy. Maybe too much. Maybe it's cooking, or fixing things, or showing up with the wrong flowers. Breathe in, and let yourself see it without embarrassment. Breathe out, and let it be enough. If you pray, you can offer your own clumsy way of loving, the hunter's way, just as it is. If not, rest in it. The bell holds the time.
Bhakti yoga, through the Nayanars: sixty-three Tamil saints of Shiva. Kannappa the hunter, who gave his eye, shows love that comes before the rules.
Your line: love as the road. Today, when someone loves you clumsily, the wrong gift, the awkward hug, receive it the way Shiva received the hunter. Day two hundred seventy.

howItsDone: In Tamil Shaiva temples, hymns of the Nayanars (the Tevaram and others) are sung daily, images of the sixty-three saints often line the temple halls, and the Periya Puranam's stories, like Kannappa's, are retold at festivals and to children.

original.note: Tamil: nayanmar, the Nayanars, 'leaders' or 'masters'; the sixty-three Tamil saints of Shiva.

trapdoor: what you thought: to worship properly, you have to know the rules.
what it means: in the Nayanar stories, love that breaks the rules is received, and even honored.

what a scholar hears: Kannappa's story is set at Kalahasti (in today's Andhra Pradesh); the Tevaram of Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar was compiled into the Tirumurai, the Tamil Shaiva canon, which closes with Sekkizhar's Periya Puranam.
